content: 1. Transitioning from merely expressing interest in voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) to actually undergoing the procedure requires sustained and targeted efforts, rather than relying on a single educational event. This includes persistent follow-up and engagement with individuals who initially show interest. 2. Quality assurance and quality improvement initiatives for VMMC were implemented to ensure the delivery of high-quality services. These efforts contributed to achieving excellence in service provision. 3. Interventions included intensive follow-up for wound care, comprehensive prevention strategies, age-appropriate sexual and reproductive health education, promotion of gender norms and condom use, escorted and supportive linkage to care and treatment for HIV-positive clients, and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for men at higher risk of HIV infection. 4. Between March 2013 and February 2019, ICAP supported 15 healthcare clinics providing facility-based VMMC services and two mobile clinics to extend services to rural areas. To generate demand, ICAP conducted age-specific outreach, including mass media campaigns and educational sessions in schools and community events. 5. Among those circumcised, 43% were adolescents and young men aged 15–24 years. Additionally, 84% of clients were screened for HIV, and 77% of those screened tested positive for HIV. Of those testing positive, 47% were enrolled in care and treatment services. 6. Targeted demand generation strategies were effective in increasing the number of older men undergoing circumcision. The use of mobile clinics ensured that VMMC services reached communities that were not easily accessible to healthcare facilities. 7. Ensuring that men who express interest in VMMC eventually undergo the procedure requires consistent and longitudinal engagement. Community-based VMMC champions played a critical role in educating and ensuring follow-up for older men. 8. A rapid assessment conducted in November 2016 revealed that fear of pain was a significant barrier to accessing VMMC services. This fear was exacerbated by misinformation spread by circumcised men and a general lack of adequate information about the procedure. Additionally, there was a lack of comprehensive training for counselors, challenges with communication materials, unmet information needs of younger clients, and underutilization of community radio. 9. To address these challenges, initiatives focused on personalized community mobilization, targeting secondary and tertiary schools, public events, and festivals. Individual follow-up was conducted afterward to ensure engagement. 10. Community mobilizers, who were circumcised men with secondary education and aged over 20 years, were hired and trained in delivering VMMC messages tailored to clients aged 15–29 years. Supervisors provided support and conducted quarterly evaluations of mobilizers’ performance, with regular refresher and on-the-job training sessions. 11. Mobilizers distributed personal invitations to men attending sessions and events, including their contact information and that of the circumcision unit, to facilitate follow-up and appointment booking. Follow-up was conducted via telephone or home visits. 12. The Decision Makers’ Program Planning Toolkit (DMPPT 2) and Geographic Information System (GIS) Mapping Dashboard were developed to assist in setting VMMC targets by age group and district, visualizing unmet needs, and aligning demand creation with service availability. These tools provided program managers with data to assess changes in VMMC uptake and evaluate the effectiveness of demand creation strategies. 13. In KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, where HIV prevalence is high and VMMC uptake is low, innovative approaches were employed to increase circumcision rates. These included endorsements by traditional leaders, mobilization campaigns in men’s hostels, informal settlements, and workplaces, and the use of mass media and online platforms. 14. Barriers to VMMC uptake in KwaZulu-Natal included a lack of knowledge about the benefits of VMMC, low perception of its relevance, and anticipated shame associated with being grouped with younger boys while awaiting services. Efforts were made to make VMMC more accessible and amplify messaging through multiple communication channels. 15. The USAID VMMC Project provided services in various settings, including public health facilities, private doctors’ practices, and VMMC camps serviced by contracted private clinical providers. These efforts were supported by endorsements from traditional leadership, including the Zulu King and his son, who actively promoted VMMC. 16. Effective recruitment, supervision, and motivation of community mobilizers were key to achieving targets. Mobilization efforts were more successful when mobilizers were assigned roles based on their abilities and background. 17. Including contact information for health units and mobilizers on invitations allowed men to ask follow-up questions and book appointments privately, enhancing engagement. 18. Mobilization in schools, particularly night courses attended by men over 15 years of age, proved effective in reaching the target age group. Similarly, mobilizing in areas with higher concentrations of women was successful, as women exert significant influence on men’s decisions. 19. Providing data on unmet needs, epidemiological impact, and service delivery capacity, visualized graphically or on maps, helped program planners focus demand creation and service delivery efforts where they were most needed and impactful. 20. Utilizing demographic models combined with program data enabled the creation of metrics to assess changes in VMMC uptake by age group, facilitating targeted interventions and improved program outcomes.
